content: Gilles de la Tourette syndrome, commonly referred to as Tourette’s syndrome, is characterized by the presence of both motor and vocal (phonic) tics that persist for more than 12 months. These symptoms must begin before the age of 18 and occur in the absence of any secondary causes. Treating motor and phonic tics in this condition is notably complex and challenging. The objective of this study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of botulinum toxin in managing motor and phonic tics in individuals with Tourette’s syndrome. Additionally, the study aimed to assess the impact of botulinum toxin on premonitory urges and sensory tics. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Movement Disorders Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and two trial registries, up to October 25, 2017. Reference lists of pertinent articles were also reviewed to identify additional trials. The inclusion criteria for this review encompassed all randomized, controlled, double-blind studies that compared botulinum toxin to either placebo or other medications for the treatment of motor and phonic tics in Tourette’s syndrome. Both parallel group and cross-over study designs were considered, involving children or adults, at any dosage, and for any treatment duration. Standard Cochrane methodologies were employed to select studies, assess the risk of bias, and extract and analyze data. All authors independently abstracted data using standardized forms, and any disagreements were resolved through discussion. Only one randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind cross-over study met the selection criteria for this review. This study enrolled 20 participants with motor tics over a three-year recruitment period, of whom 18 completed the study. Among these, 14 participants had a confirmed diagnosis of Tourette’s syndrome, and a total of 21 focal motor tics were treated. While the study was assessed to have a low risk of bias in most domains, it included a small sample size of participants with relatively mild tics, which limited the availability of data for key outcomes. The effects of botulinum toxin injections on tic frequency, as measured by videotape or subjective ratings, and on premonitory urges remain uncertain due to the very low quality of evidence. Similarly, the quality of evidence regarding adverse events associated with botulinum toxin was also very low. Nine participants experienced muscle weakness following the injections, which could have compromised the blinding of treatment group assignments. No data were available to determine whether botulinum toxin injections led to immunoresistance to the toxin. In conclusion, the effects of botulinum toxin in treating focal motor and phonic tics in select cases of Tourette’s syndrome remain uncertain due to the very low quality of evidence. Further randomized controlled studies are necessary to establish the potential benefits and risks of botulinum toxin therapy for managing motor and phonic tics in this patient population.
